thread.title: Sand In My Shoes - June Update

author: Brian Soule
title: Sand In My Shoes - June Update
text:
Another month is in the books and so is the second quarter. It is hard to believe July is here already and summer is in full swing.
June was a good month, and if you read my last update, you will know that I was basically absent for the month and this update will reflect that. No new stocks were purchased because frankly I didn't have time to research anything. I did add to my fixed income funds because they have gotten beaten up in this interest rate environment.
But even though I was not paying attention, my stocks returned over $200 to me while I was busy with other things. This is the beauty of purchasing dividend growth stocks. So let's take a look at how June treated the Sand In Shoes IRA portfolio:
June Dividends
All graphs and charts created by author unless otherwise specified
In June, total dividends paid reached $234.26, down slightly from May but still the second best total since I've started tracking them. These June dividends reflect a higher rate from both PepsiCo Inc. ( PEP ) and Southern Co. ( SO ). Also, the additional shares of 3M Co. ( MMM ) and my first dividend from Walmart Inc. ( WMT ), both purchased back in April, contributed to the nice bump.
Compared to last year, the dividends received this June are very nearly double what I received in 2017. I wish I could keep that trend up, but of course that is not possible.
I finished the first half of the year with just over $1,000 in dividends ($1,007.31). Almost certainly I will surpass $2,000 for the year, and do so fairly easily, but we'll take a look at that in a little while.
June Performance So for June I was down just slightly at 1/2 a percent on a total return basis, but again I have to stress that is not what I'm mainly searching for with this portfolio. To some investors this is anathema, but understand that I am looking for income - long-term, sustained, and increasing income - with this portfolio, not capital appreciation. This past month the portfolio kicked off nearly $1,000 of cash from all sources.
Of course, if the portfolio is built correctly, the capital appreciation will come, either through reinvesting the dividends into more shares or from the dividend increases causing the share price to increase as the yield attracts more customers (increased demand = increased price).
Individual Stocks The table below shows my positions as of close of business on June 29, 2018:
There are still three stocks with yields below 2.0%, but that is all changing as I mentioned in my last update. Both Bank of America Corp. ( BAC ) and Citigroup Inc. ( C ) just announced they plan substantial dividend hikes after the results of the Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review (CCAR) by the Fed. BAC plans to raise theirs by 25% from $0.12 to $0.15 per quarter and C plans to raise theirs 40% from $0.32 to $0.45 per quarter.
Projected Dividends As promised, here are the projected dividends for the year:
This chart shows the actual dividends collected for the first six months and the projected dividends for the 2nd half of the year. I have only included known or announced dividend hikes, but I expect another from Realty Income Corp. ( O ) and two more from Magellan Midstream Partners LP ( MMP ). Also, this does not show any additional stock purchases I might make in the coming months and the dividends associated with those new or larger positions since I don't know what I'm buying yet myself. Still, just with what is known (barring any dividend cuts) total dividends for the year will be $2,100+. That will be a successful full calendar year to me.
Sector Diversification There was not much change this month, since I did not add any new stocks. The next two sectors I will be focusing on will be utilities, where I have just Southern Co., and telecom, where I have just AT&T Inc. ( T ).
Consumer Discretionary 9.7% Consumer Staples 10.6% Energy 7.3% Financials 16.4% Health Care 10.4% Industrials 6.3% Materials 7.2% REIT 12.9% Technology 8.2% Telecom 5.2% Utilities 5.9% 100% Asset Allocation of the Portfolio
Despite my addition of roughly $1,800 to my domestic fixed income ETFs, I am still uncomfortably low in that asset class, though I am up from 27.3% last month. Though I will likely add at least one stock this month, I may also bump up my fixed income funds further. I think I mentioned in an earlier article that I do not pay transaction fees for certain ETFs, so I can add a little bit at a time until I am more balanced if necessary.
Sales and Purchases in June No sales were made of any asset. With the $1,300 in cash I had at the end of May plus the distributions I received in June, I purchased $1,800 of a domestic fixed income ETF. Not a very exciting month, but cash I receive from fixed income investments is cash I can put to work in dividend growth stocks in the future.
Final Thoughts Next month will be less than exciting as far as dividend payments go, though I will receive my first dividend from my newest addition, International Flavors & Fragrances Inc. ( IFF ).
Overall, I'm very pleased with the progress. The consistent beat-down of my fixed income investments is getting tiresome, even though I understand that interest rates are generally rising.
Next month will mark the one year point since I set the ten-year goal for myself. I will think of some way to update the progress of the goal and see if I can find my projection for where thought I would be at this point.
Thanks for reading this, and I hope you enjoy following my wife and I on our journey to financial independence. Good luck!
Disclosure: I am/we are long AAPL, AIG, AMGN, APD, BAC, BLK, C, CSCO, CVS, GPC, HD, HRL, IFF, MMM, MMP, O, OHI, PEP, SO, T, WMT.
I wrote this article myself, and it expresses my own opinions. I am not receiving compensation for it (other than from Seeking Alpha). I have no business relationship with any company whose stock is mentioned in this article.
